newsitem.title: FRANCE: French minister cautiously positive in Algeria.
newsitem.headline: French minister cautiously positive in Algeria.

text.p: Foreign Minister Hubert Vedrine, on the first visit to Algeria by a French minister in a year, said on Saturday he found the establishment of a new parliament in the strife-torn former French colony "quite encouraging".

Vedrine was in Algiers to attend a meeting of Mediterranean Forum countries, a breakthrough in Algeria's relative diplomatic isolation since the start of a bloody civil war between Islamist rebels and the military-dominated government in 1992.

The new French minister had a long private meeting with his Algerian counterpart, Ahmed Attaf. He and his colleagues from Egypt, Morocco, Tunisia and Italy were also received jointly by President Liamine Zeroual.
Vedrine stressed he had just made a first contact and had not come to negotiate.

"The brief bilateral part of my visit was mainly to find out what the situation is here after the establishement of this new assembly, where we note the existence of different parties, which is an important new element and which, seen from outside, is quite encouraging," he told France's TF1 television.

His cautiously positive comment, made in Algiers, contrasted with sharp criticism of Algeria's political system by French Socialist party leader Lionel Jospin in May, a few days before he won a parliamentary election and became prime minister.

Jospin said France should do more to promote real democracy in Algeria, which he said had a "harsh military regime". He also said Algerian elections on June 5, which gave birth to the new assembly, were not held "in sufficiently democratic conditions".
International observers criticised aspects of the elections, which legal opposition parties as well as the outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) denounced as rigged on a massive scale.
Attaf said he had called for freedom of travel for Algerians to France, which has clamped down tightly on visas to halt immigration and prevent violence spreading to French soil.

Vedrine's predecessor, Herve de Charette, tried to improve ties with a visit to Algiers last July but they were immediately overshadowed by the murder of the French-born Roman Catholic bishop of Oran, blamed by the Algerian authorities on Islamic guerrillas, hours after the minister returned to Paris.

Since then, relations have been at a virtual standstill and France has not renewed generous financial aid it gave Algiers after the military intervened in 1992 to cancel a general election which the FIS was on the verge of winning.

The former centre-right French government sought to avoid political involvement in the crisis after Algiers cancelled a planned meeting between Zeroual and President Jacques Chirac in New York in 1995, accusing France of interference for calling for greater democracy.

At least 60,000 people have died since 1992 in daily violence in Algeria. Moslem fundamentalist groups, accusing France of backing the country's military rulers, attacked French targets in Algeria and staged a wave of deadly bombings in France in 1995.
